title: No rivals: why not charge the most?
hook: A seller with no competition can pick any price. Which one earns the most?

knows: that profit is what is left after costs
that buyers buy less at a higher price
doesNotKnow: that a seller with no rivals picks a price between cost and the top of demand, and sells less than buyers would take at cost

misconception: A seller with no rival charges whatever it likes, so price is unlimited.
objective: The learner can explain that a higher price earns more per unit but loses buyers, so profit (price − cost) × units peaks in between: $60 in the model, 40 units and $1,600, against $20 and 80 units with rivals.

claims.text: If buyers pay 100 − q for the q-th unit, a single price p sells 100 − p units.
claims.source: Buyer q buys if 100 − q ≥ p, i.e. q ≤ 100 − p. Demo.tsx units().

claims.text: With a $20 cost per unit, profit (p − 20)(100 − p) is largest at $60: 40 × 40 = $1,600.
Below $60 a higher price adds more profit than the lost sales cost; above $60 the lost sales cost more.
claims.source: d/dp (p − 20)(100 − p) = 120 − 2p, positive below 60, negative above.

claims.text: With rivals undercutting each other, the price falls to the $20 cost: 80 units are sold and profit is zero.
claims.source: Textbook result for price competition with identical constant costs (Bertrand), e.g. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 15–17; units(20) = 80. Shown in the reveal only if the learner pressed 'Rivals arrive'.

claims.text: The lone seller sells fewer units (40) than buyers would take at cost (80).
The lesson is a model: straight-line demand, one price for every unit, no regulation; it takes no view on any real firm.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Model: one seller, straight-line buyers'.

recall.question: A seller with no competitors raises its price. Why might its profit fall?
options: It can't: with no rivals, a higher price always earns more
The higher margin can be outweighed by the buyers it loses
recall.why: Profit is margin times units sold. Past the best price, each rise loses more in sales than it gains per unit.
